reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes OneCoin as a financial opportunity and directs viewers to join a team and purchase a package for purported coin-mining slots. It links multigenerational referrals to percentage bonuses and claims participants will profit regardless of circumstances, alongside millionaire and imminent-growth messaging. It urges viewers to secure a position and sign up through an inviter, although it does not establish actual payments, mining, profits, or participant outcomes.

opening.argument: Judge the offer by the terms it actually states. The speaker says participants need not recruit hundreds of people or make regular monthly payments, and later says there are no monthly payments required to remain qualified to earn. Viewers are also directed to further information about the packages and compensation plan and told to contact their inviter with questions. Those details do not verify the promised profits, but an unverified promise alone does not establish that the speaker is concealing the terms of participation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution is right that tokens can be exchanged for mining slots, but that quote identifies what a package is said to contain; it does not show that the slots are fictitious or that a purchaser loses money. The referral language likewise describes a possible source of income, not proof that recruitment is the only way to participate. The speaker explicitly addresses the case of someone who does not recommend others.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of monthly fees is not a risk warning. The pitch tells viewers to purchase a package whose tokens buy mining slots, then asserts that they will profit whatever happens. It also urges them to sign up immediately. Direct purchase, assured profit and urgency are more probative of this video's purpose than an invitation to ask the seller questions.

opening.argument: Much of the presentation teaches a basic account of digital currency: it walks through earlier forms of money, describes mining as computers running algorithms, and identifies a training program for learning to trade. A viewer can understand the package discussion as part of an explanation of how this particular offering operates. The invitation to join is real, but it does not erase the substantial instructional content or itself demonstrate that the described mining is false.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution quotes the mining-slot offer and promised growth, but neither quote demonstrates whether coins were mined or what purchasers received. Its own opening acknowledges that participant outcomes are not established. Explaining a paid program and advocating for it may coexist with instruction; the quoted passages alone do not settle whether the underlying activity worked as described.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The introductory explanation leads directly to a paid mining opportunity. The speaker tells viewers to purchase a trading package, says its tokens buy mining slots, promises profit even without referrals, and ends with an immediate sign-up command. Calling the introduction educational does not change the transaction the video is trying to induce.

opening.argument: The video describes a package combining education, tokens and a rewards program. It openly describes a bonus for introducing someone and points viewers to further compensation-plan information. Referral bonuses and loyalty points can be features of ordinary promotions; their presence does not, by itself, establish that the advertised service is fictitious. The supplied presentation asks people to sign up and pay, but does not show an actual payment, a failed withdrawal or a participant's loss. Those missing outcomes matter when assessing what the video itself proves.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution correctly identifies a package payment and mining-slot claim, but it cites no completed payment or participant outcome. Nor does the existence of a referral bonus make every package purchase a recruitment-only transaction: the speaker expressly discusses participation without recommending anyone. The question is whether the available evidence proves a deceptive mechanism, not merely whether the promotion offers incentives.

citations.quote: With five education packages available all which contain tokens, which you can then exchange to buy mining slots for producing one coins
even if you decide not to recommend us to others

true_side_reply.rebuttal: This is more than a routine loyalty offer. Purchasing a package is presented as the route to tokens for mining slots, while the compensation pitch includes a binary-system payment on team business volume and matching bonuses through four generations. The speaker also promises profit regardless of whether the purchaser recruits. A recorded loss is not necessary to recognize that the video promotes paid mining returns and tiered recruitment income.
